chapter_theme: Kurinji: the secret love of the millet field on the hill, from the sweet days of guarding and the hunter's pretext (11-15) to the end of the guarding and the dangers of his night path, which the friend turns into a plea for marriage (12, 16-19), and the veri rite the mother holds because no one knows the cause (20).

11.reading: The friend reminds the soft-breasted girl that the few days they spent hidden in the millet field, while the lord of the good hill dressed her beauty in the flowering grove of gold-clustered vengai, have gone by, sweet because no one was there to give them orders.
11.nuance: போயின, 'they have gone', makes the memory a farewell: the secret days lasted only while the girls were sent to the field, and ஏயினார் இன்றி, with none to command, names the freedom that the return home will take away. The colophon gives no thurai; the speaker and addressee are inferred from மென்முலையாய் and the shared 'we'.

thinai_evidence.note: the vengai grove and the millet field of the good hill

comparisons.tenor: the yellow flower clusters of the vengai

12.reading: The friend tells the lord of the great hill that their natural task of guarding the bending millet is over, and points him to their home: this village, where the clean waterfall washes the flowers on the slope and gold is found, is where they live.
12.nuance: With the guarding over, the field can no longer be the meeting place; telling him where the house is, பாக்கம் இது எம் இடம், moves his courting from the field to the family's door, which is where marriage is asked. பாக்கம் and புறவு are usually words of the shore and the woodland; here they only name a hill village and its slope.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill and its millet field

13.reading: The friend tells the doe-eyed girl not to be bewildered by the thought that the man of the forest country will not come to embrace her shoulders: when they bathe in the white waterfall that comes down the good hill mingled with musk, her loneliness will not stay.
13.nuance: The bathing place in the falls is a meeting place, so the comfort is practical: the loneliness will leave because he will be there. The water that comes 'mixed with musk' carries the scent of his hill down to her.

thinai_evidence.note: the forest country and the hill waterfall

14.reading: The friend tells the gold-like girl in her leaf skirt that while they were guarding the millet on the slope the man came, like hunters who come asking after a beast, and that there is something else he has come to ask them.
14.nuance: The friend names the hunter's question about the animal as a manner of coming (போல), so she has already seen through the pretext: his real question, ஒன்றுண்டு, is left unsaid for the girl to guess. வினைவாய்த்து in line 2 is hard to construe; the reading takes it with his coming.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill slope and its millet field

comparisons.tenor: the man's approach to the millet field

15.reading: The friend explains that the red-lined eyes of the gentle-spoken girl have reddened because they plucked fragrant vengai flowers on the hill till their mango-shoot bodies sweated and then bathed again and again in the leaping waterfall.
15.nuance: The poem speaks of the girl in the third person (பணிமொழிக்கு) and offers a cause for her red eyes, which suggests the friend is answering an elder who has noticed them; the bath in the falls is an innocent explanation for eyes reddened by love or weeping. The addressee is inferred: the colophon gives no thurai.

thinai_evidence.note: vengai flowers and a waterfall on the hill

16.reading: Remembering the path where an elephant with folded ears, having escaped the curve-striped tiger, sits down hurt and shrinks aside in fear at the sound of footsteps, the girl with bright bangles cannot sleep through the thick dark.
16.nuance: வேங்கை here is the tiger, not the tree. The elephant that has survived the tiger and still flinches at a footfall measures the path the man takes at night; a reader may hear the girl's own fear in it, but the beast only shows the danger, so it is scene, not iraicchi. Telling him she lies awake is a way of asking him to stop the night visits and marry.

thinai_evidence.note: tiger and elephant on the night path of the hill

17.reading: The friend tells the lord of the rich hill with cloud-climbed groves that, thinking he will come without fail and afraid for him, the girl with the honeyed garland loses her bloom and soft grace and her body shrinks as she stands melting within.
17.nuance: The wasting here comes not from his absence but from his coming: எஞ்சாது நீ வருதி, you come without fail, is what she fears. His faithfulness to the night meetings is itself the harm, so only marriage would end it.

thinai_evidence.note: cloud-wrapped groves of the rich hill

18.reading: The friend tells the lord of the great hill with roaring falls that now not even the parrot flocks come, even by mistake, to the moist-eared millet that their kin cleared and ploughed, and asks him not to forget, but to keep in his heart, his bond with the gentle-spoken girl.
18.nuance: மறந்தும், 'even by forgetting', and நீ மறவல், 'do not forget', answer each other across the poem. With no parrots to chase, the girls will not be sent to the field, so the meetings there end; the friend asks that the bond outlast the field.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill millet field and its parrots

iraicchi.act: the parrot flocks stop coming to the field once there is nothing in it for them
iraicchi.sense: the man, whose meetings in the field are ending too, must not stop coming and forget her as the parrots forget the field

19.reading: The friend tells the lord of the tall hill that when he comes at midnight along the cruel path, with only his long spear for company, swimming across the fierce white waterfall, her heart asks what will become of the girl with the cool garland.
19.nuance: The friend does not say she fears for him: her heart asks what will become of the girl if harm meets him. His danger is counted as the girl's, which is the friend's way of pressing for marriage without naming it.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill waterfall crossed at midnight

20.reading: The girl says the man of the fragrant hill has taken her body's true nature, but the velan, not knowing this, declares that a spirit has seized her, drags a kid and scatters its blood, and her mother, having brought him, whirls distraught in the veri rite.
20.nuance: அறியான் is masculine: the one who does not know is the velan, whose whole office is to know the cause. அணங்கு அணங்கிற்று, 'a spirit has seized her', is true in a way he cannot see: the afflicting beauty is the hill man's. Spoken to the friend, the complaint is meant to reach the man and hurry the marriage, though the colophon gives no thurai to say he overhears.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill man and the velan's veri rite

links.note: Natrinai 259: the friendship made with the hill lord in the millet field, chasing parrots and bathing in the falls by the vengai slope, now looks hard to keep because the millet heads have ripened dry. Ainthinai Aimpathu 11: the few days in the vengai grove of the millet field have gone, sweet because no one gave orders.
links.teaches: Natrinai gives the crop's ripening as the reason the meetings end and Ainthinai names what made them possible, the absence of anyone to command the girls, so together they show the secret love as lent by the harvest calendar and taken back by it.

links.note: In Akananuru 38 the friend imagines the hill man finding the swing, the pool and the reaped field empty, and regrets that she forgot to tell him 'the high hill crowned with that white waterfall is our village'. Ainthinai Aimpathu 12 is that telling: the guarding is over, and this village by the clean waterfall is our place.
links.teaches: The longer poem shows the cost of not telling him where the house is when the field closes, and the quatrain makes the telling itself, so the pair shows pointing out the village by its waterfall as the friend's expected move at harvest, the step that turns field meetings toward the house.

links.note: In Natrinai 213 the man asks the girls which is the small rock-fenced village near the roaring falls, and whether the guarding of the millet is theirs too. In Ainthinai Aimpathu 12 the friend says their guarding of the millet is over and this village by the waterfall is their place.
links.teaches: The man's question and the friend's answer use the same two markers, the waterfall village and the guarding of the millet, which shows the exchange as a set dialogue of kurinji courtship in which the friend's answer comes only when the guarding has ended.

links.note: Akananuru 388: a young hunter with a hound comes to the millet platform asking whether a wounded tusker has passed through their field. Ainthinai Aimpathu 14: he came like those who ask after a beast, but there is something else he means to ask.
links.teaches: Akananuru stages the hunter's question in full while Ainthinai compresses it into a simile, 'like those who ask after a beast', which shows that the asking-after-game approach was a recognised pretext the girls themselves could name and see through.

links.note: Natrinai 44: the man remembers the girl after she bathed in the falls with her companions, her large eyes reddened by the beating water. Ainthinai Aimpathu 15: the friend says the girl's red-lined eyes reddened because they bathed in the leaping falls after plucking vengai.
links.teaches: The eyes reddened by the waterfall are a cherished sight for the lover in Natrinai and an explanation offered to others in Ainthinai, so the same bath serves both the love and its concealment, which is why it is safe for the friend to name.

links.note: Akananuru 308: a tusker worn from fighting a tiger, its long wound unwashed, marks the hill of a man who comes by night; the friend asks him to come by day. Ainthinai Aimpathu 16: an elephant that escaped the tiger shrinks at every footfall on the path, and the girl cannot sleep remembering that path.
links.teaches: In Akananuru the tiger-wounded elephant only marks the hill while the friend argues for day visits, whereas Ainthinai carries the beast's after-fear onto the path itself and into the girl's sleepless eyes, showing how the same hill emblem can move from scenery to the measure of a lover's dread.

links.note: Natrinai 151: even if the girl's forehead pales and her shoulders grow thin, may the hill lord not come by night. Ainthinai Aimpathu 17: because he comes without fail, the girl, afraid for him, loses her bloom and wastes away.
links.teaches: Natrinai offers her wasting as the lesser harm to be borne so that he stays away at night, but Ainthinai shows the night visits themselves causing the wasting through fear, so neither his coming nor his staying away spares her and only marriage can.

links.note: Natrinai 306: the millet is being reaped and the hill girl sent home; how will he come now to see her? Ainthinai Aimpathu 18: not even the parrots come to the millet field now; do not forget your bond with her.
links.teaches: Natrinai states the practical loss at harvest, no place left to meet, and Ainthinai names the risk behind it, that like the parrots he may stop coming once the field is empty, so the pair shows the end of the guarding feared as a test of his memory as well as of access.

links.note: In Natrinai 104 the girl asks whether anyone but her thinks of the narrow midnight path he takes while thunder strikes and floods block the way. In Ainthinai Aimpathu 19 the friend, picturing him swimming the falls at midnight, says her heart asks what will become of the girl.
links.teaches: The girl fears the night path for the man, and the friend fears it for the girl who would not survive his harm, so the pair shows the danger of the night meeting passing through two hearts, with the friend's fear one step removed and therefore usable as an argument for marriage.

links.note: In Akananuru 388 the old velan says 'my lord's seizure brought this sickness; I know the cure', and the girl mocks him. In Ainthinai Aimpathu 20 the velan, not knowing that the hill man took her nature, says a spirit has seized her and sheds the kid's blood.
links.teaches: Akananuru lets the velan claim knowledge of the cure and Ainthinai calls him plainly the one who does not know, so together they show the veri rite built around the diviner's ignorance, with the girl's secret as the one thing his craft cannot read.

source_issues: 11-20: the colophons give the thinai (குறிஞ்சி) and the poet but no thurai; every speaker and addressee in thurai_akam is inferred from the verse, with occasion words left null.
11 line 1: சவினிய is not a common word; read as 'made lustrous, in bloom' (from சவி), describing the vengai. Line 4 ஏயினார் is read as those who would order or direct the girls.
12 line 3: பூக்கண் கழூஉம் புறவிற்றாய் is hard to construe; read as 'having a slope where the waterfall washes the flowers'.
14 line 2: வினைவாய்த்து does not construe easily with the rest; taken with his coming.
16 line 1: கோட் பட்டு is unclear (seized, or struck); read as the elephant having been caught by the tiger and escaped hurt.
15: whose eyes and to whom the friend speaks are not stated; the verse is marked uncertain.
